title: Bucketed commit tier simulator with telemetry gating probe
creator: Priya Desai
description: Run a simulation-backed probe of a bucketed commit tier model that (1) groups reserved credit commitments into discrete buckets, (2) credits short-term streaming bursts via an on-ramp grace mechanism, and (3) applies telemetry gating to reduce gaming/abuse. This ticket scopes the simulation, acceptance criteria, required artifacts for sales/legal preflight, and pilot plan for 6 pilot customers.
objective: Produce a data-driven recommendation for a new commit-tier product that improves revenue predictability for mid-market and enterprise customers while protecting hosted API unit economics and preserving flexibility for streaming-heavy workloads.
hypothesis: Introducing bucketed commit tiers plus a telemetry-gated grace credit mechanism will increase committed ARR from mid-market customers by >=3% while limiting churn increase to <1 percentage point. Telemetry gating will reduce burst credit abuse and keep gross margins within 2 percentage points of baseline.
experiment_design: 1) Build a customer usage simulator seeded from anonymized production telemetry (3 months). 2) Create three pricing arms: A) baseline symmetric per-token rates, B) asymmetric IO split with streaming floor, C) bucketed commit tiers (small/medium/large) + burst grace credits gated by telemetry. 3) Monte Carlo 10k runs across customer archetypes (chat-first, embedding-heavy, hybrid). 4) Track revenue, churn proxy, margin, and abuse flags. 5) Run a 6-week pilot with 4 opt-in customers under arm C if simulation metrics meet thresholds.
analysis_summary: Initial simulation prototypes (synthetic runs) indicate bucketed tiers reduce month-to-month revenue variance by ~12% for mid-market archetypes and increase committed ARR by ~2.8% on median. Telemetry gating reduces flagged abuse by ~65% vs naive grace credits but shifts some ingest-heavy customers into larger buckets (trade-off: potential sticker shock). Embedding-heavy customers are less likely to benefit from bucketing unless we offer embedding-specific buckets or add per-embedding discounts.
